lesson.title: Big Numbers, Friendly Tricks: Adding and Subtracting to 10 000

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Last fall your school sold hot chocolate and raised two thousand four hundred fifty dollars for new playground swings. In the spring, the pancake breakfast raised one thousand three hundred seventy-five dollars more. To tell the whole school how much money they have, somebody has to add two big numbers together. That's exactly what we're learning today.

Here's the secret about big numbers: they are not scary, they are just made of smaller friendly pieces. Two thousand four hundred fifty is really two thousands, four hundreds, five tens, and zero ones. When we split a number into its places like this, big adding turns into easy adding.

visual.caption: Two thousand four hundred fifty, taken apart

steps.say: Now we add place by place, like sorting laundry into piles. Two thousands plus one thousand makes three thousand. Four hundreds plus three hundreds makes seven hundred. Five tens plus seven tens makes one hundred twenty. And zero ones plus five ones makes five. Look at that tens pile — ten of the tens grouped together and became a whole hundred! That grouping is called regrouping.

visual.caption: The tens and ones came to 125: one hundred, two tens, five ones

steps.say: Last step, we put the piles back together. Three thousand plus seven hundred plus one hundred twenty plus five gives three thousand eight hundred twenty-five. The school raised three thousand eight hundred twenty-five dollars. Those swings are getting close!

Before you ever do the careful work, do a quick guess — we call it estimating. Say a hike is three thousand eight hundred sixty metres one way and two thousand two hundred forty metres back. Three thousand eight hundred sixty is really close to four thousand, and two thousand two hundred forty is close to two thousand. Four thousand plus two thousand is about six thousand metres. Now if your careful answer came out as sixty thousand, you'd know right away something went wrong.

visual.caption: 3 860 hops over to its friendly neighbour, 4 000

steps.say: Subtracting has a lovely trick too, called using a friendly number. Your family has four thousand dollars saved for a trip, and the ferry and flights cost one thousand nine hundred ninety-eight dollars. Instead of that bumpy nine-nine-eight, pretend it costs a friendly two thousand. Four thousand take away two thousand is two thousand. But wait — you pretended you paid two dollars too much, so give those two dollars back. Two thousand and two dollars are left.

visual.caption: Round it, subtract it, then pay yourself back the extra $2

steps.say: Let's try one a little harder. Your school's big goal is ten thousand dollars, and so far you have six thousand four hundred seventy-five. Instead of borrowing across all those zeros, just hop up the number line. From six thousand four hundred seventy-five, hop twenty-five to reach six thousand five hundred. Hop five hundred more to reach seven thousand. Then one big hop of three thousand lands on ten thousand. Add your hops: twenty-five plus five hundred plus three thousand is three thousand five hundred twenty-five dollars still to go. And it checks out, because six thousand four hundred seventy-five plus three thousand five hundred twenty-five is exactly ten thousand.

visual.caption: Hop up in friendly jumps: 25, then 500, then 3 000

steps.say: So remember, big numbers are just piles of thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Guess first, then take the numbers apart in whichever way feels friendliest to you. There isn't only one right path — there's the path that makes sense in your head. Great work today!

lesson.answer: Break big numbers into friendly pieces, estimate first, then add or subtract piece by piece — and check your answer against your guess.

practice.question: A hockey arena in Kelowna holds 6 000 people. On Saturday night, 4 275 seats were filled. First estimate how many seats were empty, then work out the exact number.
practice.answer: Estimate: 4 275 is close to 4 300, and 6 000 minus 4 300 is about 1 700 empty seats. Exact: 6 000 minus 4 275 equals 1 725 empty seats. (Check by hopping up: 4 275 plus 25 is 4 300, plus 700 is 5 000, plus 1 000 is 6 000 — that's 25 plus 700 plus 1 000 equals 1 725.) The estimate of about 1 700 was very close, so the answer makes sense.
